title: Service documentation
audience: Home-based property managers and property manager partner workers who record services and maintenance for properties
learningOutcomes: Use a standard checklist for each service visit so that records are comparable across properties.
Record the service, the findings and the next action in a form the owner can read.
Store service records so they can be retrieved for each asset and each property.
referencesAtStart: Official sources: none checked for this lesson. The record practice here is working practice, not a regulatory rule.

instruction.heading: Standard checklists make records comparable
instruction.body: Each type of service has its own checklist. The checklist lists what is checked, what is done, what is found, and what is due next. A standard form means that the owner can compare visits across properties, and a new worker can pick up a record without asking the last person what they meant. Keep the checklist short enough to complete on site, with space for brief notes and photographs. Each entry needs a date, the name of the worker, and the asset identifier from the register. Where a checklist item is not applicable to the visit, mark it as not applicable and give the reason, rather than leaving it blank. A blank field looks the same as a missed check, and the reader cannot tell which it is.

instruction.heading: Asset identifiers and the register
instruction.body: Give every asset in the portfolio an identifier, such as a code on a label, and record that identifier in the asset register. An air conditioning unit, a hot water system, a gate operator and a pool pump are all assets. Use the identifier on every service entry, so the history of one item can be pulled from its own file. Where two items of the same type sit in one property, the identifiers keep them apart. If an asset is replaced, record the date, the old identifier and the new one, and keep the history of the old asset on file. Do not merge the history of a replaced asset into the new one.

instruction.heading: Store, retrieve and correct the record
instruction.body: File each service record against the property and against each asset, so that both views work. Keep the original record. When an error is found, record the correction as a dated addition that states what was wrong and what the correct entry is. Do not overwrite or delete the original. Set a retention period for records in line with the owner's requirements and the applicable rules. Keep records secure, and limit access to people who need them for the job.

instruction.heading: Readable summaries for the owner
instruction.body: The owner reads a summary, and the detail stays on file. A useful summary states the property, the asset, the service, the date, what was found, what was done, and what is due next. Use plain words, and avoid technical shorthand that the owner has to decode. Where a photograph supports the summary, include it only with the owner's permission and only if it shows the asset or the finding and nothing personal. Send the summary within an agreed time after the visit. A summary that cannot be checked against the detail on file should not be sent.

instruction.heading: A service record is not a regulated certificate
instruction.body: A service record shows what a worker checked and did. It does not replace a certificate, report or compliance record that a regulator or a licensed trade issues. Where a regulated service needs a certificate, the licensed trade or authorised person issues it, and the service record refers to that certificate by its number and date. This lesson does not give the worker authority to issue, sign or certify any regulated service, and the worker must not describe a service record as a certificate.

procedure: Use the standard checklist for the service type.
Record what was checked, what was done, what was found and what is due next, marking any item not applicable with the reason.
Date the entry, name the worker and record the asset identifier from the register.
File the record against the property and against the asset.
Correct any error by a dated addition that states the correction, and keep the original.
Send the owner a readable summary of the service, with photographs only where the owner has agreed.
Refer any regulated certificate to the licensed trade or authorised person, and record its number and date when it is issued.

workedExamples.situation: An owner asks for the service history of one air conditioning unit across three properties.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How can the history be found quickly and reliably?
workedExamples.reasoning: If each record is filed against the asset identifier from the register, the history of each unit can be pulled from its own file. Check that the identifier on each entry matches the register before sending the history. Send the owner a readable summary of each visit, and keep the detail on file. If one entry has no identifier, record a dated correction that adds it, with a note of how it was matched, and do not guess.

workedExamples.situation: A worker finds a service entry for a gate operator with no asset identifier. The entry was made last month.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should be done with the entry?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not delete it and do not overwrite it. Check the register and the property record to find the identifier for the gate operator at that address. Add a dated correction to the entry that records the identifier and how it was matched. If the identifier cannot be confirmed, record that as an open item and tell the supervisor. Do not file the entry against a different asset.

equipmentAndPpe: Standard service checklist for each service type
Filing or digital record system, with access restricted to people who need it
Camera or phone for photographs, used only with the owner's permission

commonErrors.error: Using a different format for each visit.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the standard checklist for each service type.

commonErrors.error: Filing a record without an asset identifier.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the asset identifier from the register on every entry, and correct any missing identifier by dated addition.

commonErrors.error: Overwriting a record to correct it.
commonErrors.prevention: Add a dated correction that states the change, and keep the original.

commonErrors.error: Describing a service record as a certificate.
commonErrors.prevention: State the record as a record. Refer any regulated certificate to the licensed trade or authorised person.

commonErrors.error: Sending the owner photographs that show personal items or other people.
commonErrors.prevention: Send only photographs the owner has agreed to, cropped to the asset or the finding.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Certificates and compliance records for regulated services are issued by the licensed trade or authorised person. A service record does not replace a certificate that a regulator requires. Where a regulated service is done, the record refers to the certificate by its number and date.
Completing this lesson does not give a licence or authority to certify any service, and it does not authorise the worker to sign a compliance record.
Check the owner's requirements and the applicable rules before setting a retention period.

qualityStandard: Every service uses the standard checklist for its type, and each item is completed or marked not applicable with a reason.
Every entry is dated, names the worker and records the asset identifier from the register.
Corrections are dated additions, and the original is retained.
Every owner summary matches the detail on file.
documentationEvidence: Completed service checklist for each visit
Filed record against the property and against the asset
Dated correction for each error found, with the original retained
Readable summary sent to the owner, with any agreed photographs
summary: Use one checklist for each service type so that records compare across properties.
File every record against the asset identifier, and correct it by a dated addition, never by overwriting.
Send a readable summary to the owner, and keep the detail on file.
A service record is not a regulated certificate, and the worker does not certify regulated work.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is each service record filed against the asset identifier?
options: So the history of a single item can be found reliably
To make the file thicker and look more complete
Because owners ask for it in a random order
It is not needed once the visit is complete

knowledgeChecks.question: A record has an error. What should be done?
options: Overwrite the entry with the correct details so the record is neat
Delete the entry and start the record again from the beginning
Add a dated correction that states the change, and keep the original
Ask the owner to ignore it and carry on with the record as normal

knowledgeChecks.question: A service visit involves a regulated item. What does the service record do?
options: It replaces the certificate that the regulator requires for the item on the site
It refers to the certificate issued by the licensed trade, by its number and date
It is signed by the worker as a certificate of the work done on the job today and dated
It is kept only on the worker's phone and not in the property file at all, ever
